The rigid function family is defined by the linear PDE $f''(x) = 0$, which implies that the function space is strictly linear ($f(x) = ax+b$), and this low-dimensional manifold allows small-width neural networks to achieve zero violation on held-out points as $w$ increases.

The generalization error (heldout_err) of the rigid family is dominated by the transport of error from the training region to the held-out region in the input space, and this transport is governed by a Lipschitz continuity constraint that limits the function's slope, effectively acting as a regularizer that reduces the effective capacity of the network.

The "fat" family's failure to achieve zero violation is due to the composition of its basis functions (e.g., high-degree polynomials) creating a condition number that explodes as the number of samples $w$ increases, making the inverse problem ill-conditioned and preventing the network from converging to a solution that satisfies all constraints, regardless of width.
